newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Japan focus on Tokyo aluminium, yen.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Japan focus on Tokyo aluminium, yen.

text.p: Japan's metal markets were quiet following an import rush earlier this month, with participants focused on the launch of Tokyo aluminium futures trading and the yen's slide against the dollar, traders said on Wednesday.
"The markets are very quiet," said one trader. "Nobody's willing to buy metals from overseas at these yen levels."

On Wednesday the dollar continued its recent advance against the yen, rising nearly to 127 yen, its highest since August 1992, on the backdrop of widening interest rate gaps between Japan and United States.
Traders said the dollar's rise came after heavy imports at the start of the month under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme more than covered demand.

"There were no big deals after the GSP imports," said one copper trader. The scheme grants a tariff exemption to developing country imports submitted for customs clearance at the beginning of the fiscal year on April 1.
Data released last week showed larger-than-expected imports of 75,631 tonnes of refined copper and 112,639 tonnes of refined zinc at the beginning of fiscal 1997/98.
Traders noted few spot copper deals apart from small-lot buying from China, although recent price declines may encourage Chinese buyers to enter the market.
One trader said a possible ban on imports of secondary copper in China was unlikely to have a significant impact on the primary market.

In Shanghai on Tuesday, a U.S. Chamber of Commerce official said that a potential ban on exports of some secondary raw materials from most OECD member countries could slash China's secondary copper imports beginning in 1998.

In the aluminium market, spot trade remained slack and traders monitored activity in Tokyo's yen-based aluminium futures, which started trading on Monday. Price declines on the Tokyo Commodity Exchange on the first day of trading helped spark a sell-off by funds overseas.
"Obviously we are all watching the futures market, although at the moment the only participants are speculators and trade houses doing arbitrage business," said one trader.

The Tokyo aluminium futures market recovered modestly after its initial plunge on Monday, while volume continued to decline from 19,645 lots on the first day. A total of 5,334 lots changed hands on Wednesday, down from 8,290 on Tuesday.
While most traders said physical aluminium premiums were unchanged from the week before, one said some deals might have taken place at levels below $80 a tonne.
The zinc market was quiet.

Although a report in the Japanese trade paper Sangyo Shimbun said that Japan's domestic demand for zinc would rise in the first half of fiscal 1997/98 due to strong demand from the car industry, traders remained cautious about the medium- and long-term outlook.
"I believe strong demand will continue throughout June, but I am worried about afterwards. The heavy GPS imports could also trigger a price decline," one zinc trader said.
